```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A transition network compresses a set of sessions into one matrix of
single-step transitions. The compression keeps the structure of the
interaction, which codes lead to which, but it discards two things that
questions about human-AI collaboration often need. The first is time: when
in a session each actor acts, whether sessions open with a long human
specification or with an immediate request, and how long each actor holds
the turn. The second is longer patterns: a human request answered by an AI
execution and followed by another request is a unit of collaboration that a
network splits into two independent edges.

This guide covers the views of a heterogeneous network that keep these
features. Sequence plots draw every session as a row of coded events, either
coloured by code or by actor. Meta-paths count recurring runs of codes and
their actor templates, such as `Human->AI->Human`, and compare them with the
frequencies expected if the codes followed each other independently.
Association rules describe which codes occur together in the same session,
regardless of order. Sequence comparison tests which patterns distinguish
two groups of sessions.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming; each row is one
coded event.

- **Session**: `session_id`; one row of a sequence plot.
- **Code**: `code`; six human codes (Specify, Request, Frustrate, Check,
  Inquire, Refine) and six AI codes (Delegate, Plan, Execute, Ask, Repair,
  Report).
- **Actor type**: `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`; the actor of each code.
- **Order**: `order_in_session`; the position of the event in its session.
- **Cohort**: `phase`, `Early` or `Late`; used for the group comparison.

```{r build}
data(human_ai)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

## How does each actor's work unfold within a session?

`sequence_plot_htna()` extracts each actor's events from every session and
draws them as one row per session and actor, coloured by code. The default
index layout has one panel per actor, with sessions ordered so that similar
sequences lie next to each other.

```{r index-state, fig.height = 5.5}
sequence_plot_htna(net)
```

The human panel is dominated by requests and specifications and the AI
panel by executions and asks; long runs of one colour along a row are the
repeated moves that appear as self-transitions in the network. The legend is
split by actor, so each code is read under the actor that owns it.

The distribution layout summarizes the same information over sessions: at
each position, the share of sessions in each code. Because each actor's row
is empty at the positions where the other actor acted, `na = FALSE` leaves
those positions out, so the shares are within the actor.

```{r distribution-state}
sequence_plot_htna(net, type = "distribution", na = FALSE)
```

## How do the actors take turns?

With `by = "group"`, every event of the combined session is coloured by its
actor, which turns the plot into a display of turn-taking. Rows with many
short stripes are sessions in which the actors alternate quickly; long
blocks of one colour are stretches in which one actor holds the turn.

```{r index-group, fig.height = 5.5}
sequence_plot_htna(net, by = "group")
```

The distribution layout gives the share of sessions in which each actor
acts at each position, so it shows whether either actor dominates the
openings or the later stages of the sessions.

```{r distribution-group}
sequence_plot_htna(net, by = "group", type = "distribution")
```

The heatmap layout draws the sessions as one carpet, with the actors
separated by a white band; it compares session lengths and the uniformity
of the sessions at a glance.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 5.5}
sequence_plot_htna(net, type = "heatmap")
```

## Which turn-taking templates recur?

`extract_meta_paths()` with `level = "type"` replaces every code by its
actor and counts the resulting templates. For runs of two events, the four
templates are the four blocks of the network.

```{r meta-2}
extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 2)
```

Handovers dominate: a human event is followed by an AI event 5,970 times
and an AI event by a human event 5,693 times, against 4,674 human-human and
2,581 AI-AI pairs. The lift compares each count with the count expected if
consecutive events were independent given the overall share of each actor;
handovers occur 1.28 and 1.22 times as often as expected, continuations of
the same actor less often than expected (0.79 and 0.70). The interaction is
alternating rather than a series of monologues.

Longer templates show how the alternation is organized. For runs of four
events:

```{r meta-4}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 4), n = 8)
```

The most frequent four-event template is `AI->Human->Human->AI`, an AI move
answered by two human moves before the AI acts again (2,276 occurrences in
389 sessions, lift 2.07). Strict alternation (`AI->Human->AI->Human`, lift
1.81) is next. The human more often takes two consecutive turns between AI
moves than the AI does between human moves.

## Which concrete paths realize a template?

A `schema` restricts the search to one template and returns its concrete
instances, each with the template in `meta_schema`. Elements can be actor
types, codes or `*` for any element.

```{r schema-human}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "Human->AI->Human"), n = 8)
```

The 163 concrete paths of the `Human->AI->Human` template are led by a
request, an AI execution and another request (401 occurrences in 194
sessions, 45.2% of the sessions), which occurs five times as often as
expected (lift 5.00). The request-execute-request loop is the backbone of
these sessions. Its mirror image, the AI side of the alternation, is found
with the template `AI->Human->AI`, here restricted to paths at least twice
as frequent as expected:

```{r schema-ai}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "AI->Human->AI", min_lift = 2), n = 8)
```

`Execute->Request->Execute` is the AI-centered view of the same loop (391
occurrences, lift 4.65). The pattern with the highest lift among those shown,
`Plan->Check->Execute` (lift 6.00), is a human check between an AI plan and
its execution.

Patterns need not be contiguous. With `type = "gapped"` the elements of a
path are `gap + 1` positions apart, which describes what happens two moves
later regardless of the move in between.

```{r gapped}
extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 3, type = "gapped", gap = 1)
```

Even with one event skipped between the elements, `Human->AI->Human`
remains the most frequent template (3,265 occurrences, lift 1.35).

## Which codes occur together in a session?

Association rules ignore order and ask which codes appear together in the
same session. `association_rules_htna()` treats each session as the set of
its codes and keeps the rules above the support, confidence and lift
thresholds.

```{r rules}
rules <- association_rules_htna(net, min_support = 0.3, min_confidence = 0.8,
                                max_length = 3L)
rules
```

With support of at least 0.3 and confidence of at least 0.8, 499 rules
remain. The rules with the highest lift link the AI's `Report` to the human's
`Inquire`: sessions that contain an AI report together with a human check,
or with an AI plan, execution or ask, contain a human inquiry in more than
80% of cases (confidence 0.803 to 0.831), 1.32 to 1.37 times as often as
sessions in general. Session-level co-occurrence is a
coarser view than the paths above and complements them.

## Which patterns distinguish early from late sessions?

`sequence_compare_htna()` counts every pattern of three to five codes in two
cohorts of sessions and tests, by permuting whole sessions between the
cohorts, whether its frequency differs between them. P-values are adjusted
for the number of patterns (false discovery rate). Each pattern also has a
standardised residual per cohort (Haberman, 1973): a positive residual means
the pattern is more frequent in that cohort than independence of pattern and
cohort predicts. The permutations are random, so a seed is set first.

```{r compare}
set.seed(2026)
grp <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type", group = "phase")
res <- sequence_compare_htna(grp, sub = 3:5, min_freq = 25L, iter = 500L)
res
```

Of the 106 patterns that occur at least 25 times in each cohort, the
comparison counts how many differ at an adjusted p-value below 0.05:

```{r compare-count}
xtabs(~ p_value < 0.05, data = summary(res))
```

Thirteen patterns distinguish the cohorts. The late sessions contain more
`Request->Specify->Ask` (residual 3.73 in the late cohort) and
`Ask->Plan->Frustrate`; the early sessions contain more
`Request->Specify->Frustrate` and `Specify->Frustrate->Ask->Plan` (residuals
3.76 and 3.72 in the early cohort). Frustration therefore sits at different
points of the request-plan cycle in the two phases: before the AI asks and
plans in the early sessions, after it plans in the late ones. The pyramid
plot shows the most distinctive patterns with their counts and residuals.

```{r pyramid, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(res, style = "pyramid", show_residuals = TRUE)
```

With `level = "type"`, the comparison runs on actor templates instead of
codes.

```{r compare-type}
sequence_compare_htna(grp, level = "type", sub = 3:5, min_freq = 25L,
                      iter = 500L)
```

At the level of actor templates no pattern reaches an adjusted p-value below
0.05; the smallest is 0.0519, for `Human->Human->Human->AI->Human`, which is
about twice as frequent in the late sessions (196 against 112
occurrences). The turn-taking structure is largely the same in both phases;
what changes is which codes fill the turns.

## Which view to use

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| When does each actor do what within a session? | `sequence_plot_htna()` (index, `by = "state"`) |
| How do the actors take turns? | `sequence_plot_htna(by = "group")` |
| Which actor templates recur, and more than expected? | `extract_meta_paths(level = "type")` |
| Which concrete paths realize a template? | `extract_meta_paths(schema = )` |
| Which codes occur together in sessions? | `association_rules_htna()` |
| Which patterns distinguish groups of sessions? | `sequence_compare_htna()` |

Single transitions between cohorts are compared with the functions of the
[Comparing networks](comparing-networks.html) guide.

## References

Haberman, S. J. (1973). The analysis of residuals in cross-classified
tables. *Biometrics*, 29(1), 205-220. <https://doi.org/10.2307/2529686>
